extracted.intended_audience: students of political theory, constitutional designers, legislators, and educated readers interested in forms of government
extracted.subtask_description: Analysing and prescribing principles for stable governments — how property distribution, mixed constitutions, separation of powers, militia, and electoral design affect the generation, corruption, and preservation of republics and monarchies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of dominion in land / property distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: The balance of dominion in land is the natural cause of empire; the distribution of landed property (who holds how much) determines whether a territory tends toward monarchy, aristocracy, or a commonwealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerical thought-experiment: if one person can keep many servants by proportionate wealth, a single person or a few with large estates (e.g., owning three parts in four) can control government (absolute monarchy or aristocracy). Conversely, if the people hold the large share of territory (e.g., three parts in four), no single person or nobility can dispute government and they govern themselves. Examples: a single landlord => absolute monarchy; few landlords => aristocracy; whole people holding lands => commonwealth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preventing concentration of property early
rubrics_metrics.description: It is better to prevent the growth of concentrated wealth and landed over-balance at the beginning than to seek remedies after it has become entrenched.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remedies when concentration exists (late): agrarian laws, debt relief (recision of debts), redistribution measures. Anti-pattern: allowing estates and fortunes to grow unchecked leads to perpetual feuds and instability (e.g., Athens and Rome examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed (compound) constitution as superior
rubrics_metrics.description: The best form of government is a compound of kingly, aristocratical, and democratical elements rather than any simple form alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Polybius and Lycurgus: combining the advantages of the three forms produces mutual checks—each order (king/consuls, senate, people) restrains the others. Examples: Spartan institutions, Roman constitution where consuls (monarchical), senate (aristocratical), and people (democratical) each have significant functions. Design implication: create institutions embodying distinct functions so they can check and balance one another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate separation and distribution of powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Powers (executive, legislative, judicial, financial, military) must be distributed with sufficient accuracy so that branches can control and interpose upon each other; inadequate separation undermines a constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique: Roman executive was not sufficiently separated from the legislative; executive lacked defined power to interpose between people and senate. Design implication: define competences and interposition/arbiter powers clearly so that no branch can unilaterally dominate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checks and balances among orders
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinct orders (consuls/king, senate/aristocracy, people/democracy) must have powers enabling them to oppose, assist, and balance each other as circumstances require.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of checks: senate controls money, people distribute honours and punishments, consuls lead in war yet need senate/people support for supplies and ratification of treaties. When branches must rely on one another (e.g., generals need senate and people's consent for supplies and triumphs), collective action is strengthened and abuse constrained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fair and effective representation of the people
rubrics_metrics.description: The people must be fairly and fully represented so they possess real power of dividing, choosing, or checking other branches; otherwise the system becomes disposed of by a few.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If representation is weak or token (or if a single assembly concentrates all powers), natural aristocracy and corruption follow. Design implication: ensure representative structures give the people a meaningful share in government decisions to maintain balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electoral design must minimize corruption and undue influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Popular elections have inherent dangers: competition among candidates with similar merits leads to undue attention to bribery, entertainments, and the candidate with the deepest purse prevailing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: single assembly elections without safeguards foster a 'natural aristocracy' of those distinguished by blood/education/fortune who resort to bribery and intrigue. Design choices should limit opportunities and incentives for vote-buying and clientelism (e.g., institutional checks, staggered elections, qualification rules).

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and integrity of the nobility / gentry
rubrics_metrics.description: A nobility or gentry that over-balances a popular government is destructive; conversely, a gentry that does not over-balance is vital to the health of a popular government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the nobility alone is capable of magistracy or senatorial office, the commonwealth becomes unequal (as Rome). If the nobility attains office only by election of the people (as Sparta or Venice), the commonwealth remains equal. Design implication: prevent nobility from monopolizing ruling offices; allow mechanisms of popular election or limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citizen militia (public sword) as inseparable to liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: The public sword—the right and duty of a citizen militia—is inseparable from property balance and essential to preserving liberty; governments of citizens produce the most resilient and courageous defense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Governments of citizens (where many are landholders trained as soldiers) are hardest to conquer and hardest to hold due to unity and well-disciplined militia. Anti-pattern: standing armies under monarchies yield different vulnerabilities. Institutional implication: preserve civic military obligations and broad property-holding to sustain militia.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lifecycle / tendency to degeneracy of simple governments
rubrics_metrics.description: Every simple form of government has an implanted vice that causes it to degenerate (kingly => monarchy/tyranny, aristocracy => oligarchy, democracy => rage/violence); constitutional design must account for and mitigate these tendencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lycurgus's solution: unite the best properties of different governments so no branch can swell beyond bounds; Roman example: mixing orders delayed degeneration. Design implication: institutionalize countervailing powers and cultural/legal restraints to slow or prevent corruption via luxury, inherited privilege, or faction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic and legal regulation affecting stability
rubrics_metrics.description: Economic laws (e.g., prohibitions on usury, trade restrictions) and legal institutions regarding contracts, public works, and property materially affect the stability and equality of a commonwealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited: Israel's laws against usury and Lacedemon's laws against trade; cenfors and senate oversight of public works and contracts. Design implication: craft economic and legal rules that prevent predatory practices and limit avenues for concentration of power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocation of financial, judicial, and diplomatic powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Which body controls public money, major crimes, embassies, declarations of war, and treatment of ambassadors is a central constitutional decision shaping whether a regime leans monarchical, aristocratical, or democratical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Roman example: the senate controlled receipts and disbursements and had jurisdiction over serious crimes and foreign policy, making the government appear aristocratical; the people retained powers over honours/punishments and ratifying laws. Design implication: distribute high-leverage functions across orders to maintain balance and legitimacy.
